person.name: Konrad_Zuse
person.tagline: Builder of the first programmable computer
person.summary: Konrad Zuse was a German engineer and inventor whose relay-based Z3 (operational in 1941) is widely regarded as the first working, freely programmable, automatic digital computer. He later founded one of Germany’s earliest computer firms and pursued ideas in computing theory alongside artistic work.

portrait.caption: Stylized portrait based on historical photograph
portrait.creator: AI generated artwork

conclusion: Konrad Zuse proved that programmable machines could be built—not in a factory, but in a room full of improvised parts and stubborn clarity. From the Z3 to the founding of Zuse KG, his life traces the arc from solitary invention to a new industry, while he remained, at heart, a maker who treated technology as a form of creative work.

events.title: Born in Deutsch-Wilmersdorf (Berlin)
events.description: Konrad Ernst Otto Zuse was born on 22 June 1910 in Deutsch-Wilmersdorf (Berlin) to Maria and Emil Zuse.

images.caption: Konrad Zuse in Berlin Bundesallee; birthplace mentioned

events.title: Family settles in Hoyerswerda
events.description: In 1923, Zuse’s family moved to Hoyerswerda after earlier years in East Prussia (Braunsberg). At school there, he began tinkering seriously: by about age 14 he built “Zuses Mandarinenautomat,” a coin-operated dispenser that produced fruit and change.

events.title: Passes the Abitur
events.description: In 1928, Zuse completed his [[Abitur|Abitur]], the school-leaving qualification required for university study in Germany. The milestone cleared the way for his move to Berlin for technical education.

Abitur.explanation: The German secondary-school leaving examination/certificate that qualifies students for admission to university (higher education).

events.title: Starts at TH Berlin-Charlottenburg
events.description: In 1928, Zuse began studying at the [[Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenburg|Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenburg]] (today TU Berlin). He started in mechanical engineering, switched to architecture, and ultimately settled on civil engineering. Along the way, he also worked for nearly a year as a commercial artist, reflecting his lasting pull toward both technology and art.

Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenb.explanation: Historical name of the engineering university in Berlin-Charlottenburg that later became Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin).

events.title: Earned engineering diploma
events.description: In 1935, Zuse completed his civil engineering diploma in Berlin. He then worked as a structural analyst at Henschel Flugzeug-Werke AG in Schönefeld near Berlin, where repetitive calculations sharpened his desire to automate computation.

Henschel & Son.explanation: A major German engineering and armaments firm; its Kassel-based works included aircraft production in the 1930s and later became known for wartime manufacturing.

events.title: Builds the Z1 in his parents’ apartment
events.description: After leaving his job, Zuse set up an inventor’s workshop in his parents’ apartment in Berlin and began building a programmable calculating machine. This effort produced the Z1 (completed in 1938): a bold architectural blueprint for a computer, but not yet fully reliable in practice because it relied on mechanical parts. The core ideas would carry forward into his later machines.

images.caption: Diagrams from Zuse’s May 1936 patent (binary switching)

event_class.title: Z1
event_class.description: An electrically driven mechanical binary calculator with separate memory and control, reading programs from punched film.
event_class.impact: Introduced core computer architecture elements, though mechanical tolerances prevented reliable long-term operation.

events.title: Demonstrated Z2 prototype
events.description: In 1940, Zuse completed the Z2 as an interim step after the Z1 and demonstrated it in Berlin to influential aviation and research representatives, including Günther Bock of the [[Deutsche Versuchsanstalt für Luftfahrt|German Aeronautical Research Institute]]. The showing helped him win backing for a more capable follow-on machine.

Deutsche Versuchsanstalt für Luftfahrt.explanation: German aeronautics research body (often abbreviated DVL) that evaluated and coordinated aviation research; its support could unlock wartime funding.

event_class.title: Z2
event_class.description: An electromechanical relay-based prototype using binary fixed-point arithmetic to validate control logic, memory, and switching principles.
event_class.impact: Its successful demonstration helped unlock institutional funding and momentum for the later Z3 computer.

events.title: Unveils the Z3
events.description: On 12 May 1941, Zuse publicly presented the Z3 in Berlin. Built with relays and designed for program-controlled calculation, it is widely described as the first functioning, fully automatic, freely programmable digital computer. Zuse had also exchanged ideas with Helmut Schreyer during this period as he pushed beyond what purely mechanical designs could do.

images.caption: Replica of the Zuse Z3, Deutsches Museum Munich

Berlin.explanation: Germany’s capital; in 1941 it was the administrative center of Nazi Germany, where Zuse maintained his small engineering office during wartime.

event_class.title: Z3
event_class.description: A relay-based, program-controlled digital computer using binary floating-point arithmetic, with memory and a central processing unit.
event_class.impact: Widely regarded as the first functioning, freely programmable automatic digital computer.

events.title: War work at Henschel
events.description: During World War II, Zuse was twice conscripted but did not see combat. With help from Herbert Wagner at Henschel, he was classified as “indispensable” and continued technical work there. In this period he contributed to the Henschel Hs 293 glide bomb project and developed special-purpose calculating devices for wing measurement—wartime work that kept his computing ideas alive under tight constraints.

event_class.title: S1/S2 measurement computers
event_class.description: Special-purpose systems that mechanized instrument readings, converting analog measurement values into discrete signals for computation and control.
event_class.impact: Among the earliest practical analog-to-digital conversion approaches, enabling computer-assisted measurement and automated control.

Hs 293.explanation: German air-launched, radio-guided glide bomb developed by Henschel during World War II.

events.title: Married Gisela Brandes
events.description: On 6 January 1945, Zuse married Gisela Brandes (1919–2013) in Berlin. In the midst of collapse and displacement, the marriage became the start of a family that would later include five children.

events.title: Flees Berlin, saves the Z4
events.description: As Berlin became increasingly dangerous in the final weeks of the war, Zuse and his family fled westward. He managed to save the [[Z4]] computer, moving it first toward Göttingen and then onward into the Allgäu region. Keeping the machine intact would later prove decisive: it became the practical foundation for his postwar restart.

images.caption: Zuse Z4 computer at the Deutsches Museum, Munich

Z4.explanation: Zuse’s last wartime computer, later put to serious scientific use in Zurich in the early 1950s.

Allgäu.explanation: A cultural and geographic region in southern Germany (mainly Bavaria, extending into Baden-Württemberg).

events.title: Founded Zuse KG
events.description: In 1949, Zuse founded [[Zuse KG]] and began turning his inventions into products—an early step in rebuilding German computing after the war. In the early postwar years, the rescued Z4 also drew serious academic interest, including arrangements that brought it into scientific use at the [[ETH Zürich|ETH Zürich]] under Eduard Stiefel.

Zuse KG.explanation: Konrad Zuse’s computer company founded after WWII; it built early commercial computers and was later taken over by Siemens.

ETH Zürich.explanation: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich, a leading technical university where the Z4 was used in the early 1950s.

events.title: Lost control of Zuse KG
events.description: In 1964, after rapid expansion left Zuse KG over-indebted, Konrad Zuse had to give up his capital share—ending his role as the controlling owner of the company he had built. He continued afterward as a consultant and increasingly focused on his theoretical idea of the “Rechnender Raum.”

Zuse KG.explanation: Konrad Zuse’s computer manufacturing company (Zuse Kommanditgesellschaft), founded after WWII and based in Bad Hersfeld; it produced early commercial computers and was later taken over by Siemens.

events.title: Lectured in East Germany
events.description: In 1983, Zuse accepted an invitation that allowed him to give a public lecture in Ilmenau in the [[German Democratic Republic|German Democratic Republic]]. The moment highlighted how far his early work had traveled—even as Europe remained divided by Cold War borders.

images.caption: Campus of Ilmenau University of Technology

German Democratic Republic.explanation: East Germany (1949–1990), the Soviet-aligned state formed after World War II and separated from West Germany during the Cold War.

events.title: Death in Hünfeld
events.description: Konrad Zuse died in Hünfeld on 18 December 1995. By then he had become a living reference point for computing’s origin story—while still returning, in private, to drawing and painting alongside engineering ideas.

images.caption: Grave of Konrad Zuse in Hünfeld
